summary: VERIT-X (Viewer for Epoch-Resolved Infrared Tracking) lets anyone type a position in the sky and watch NASA's SPHEREx images of that patch play back in time. For each position it finds every SPHEREx exposure taken so far (usually 250 to 550), stacks each six-month sky pass into one frame, and plays the passes as a flipbook. Distant stars stay put while nearby stars and brown dwarfs jump. A change view subtracts the first pass. A colour view maps SPHEREx's 0.75 to 5 micrometre range onto blue, green and red, which makes cold brown dwarfs look red. A spectrum built from the individual exposures shows what an object is made of. On every challenge target that moves, the object sits where its published proper motion says it should be. It matters because nearby, hard-to-see objects such as cold brown dwarfs, and possibly undiscovered planets, give themselves away by moving, and SPHEREx now photographs the whole sky every six months. This tool gives anyone a way to look.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

VERIT-X is a public website. You pick one of the five test objects named in the challenge, or (on the local version) type any sky coordinates. The site shows that patch of sky once for every six-month pass SPHEREx has made over it, three or four so far, and flips through them like a short video. Background stars stay still. Anything near us jumps. Around that core it offers a change view, a choice of infrared wavelength, an infrared colour view, a spectrum of the object, an overlay of catalogued stars, the object's predicted path, shareable links, and a record of how many images went into each frame and how many were affected by saturation or optical ghosts.

THE CONCEPTS BEHIND IT

1. Writing down a position in the sky. Astronomers use two angles, like longitude and latitude. Right ascension runs around the sky and is written in hours, minutes and seconds (24 hours make a full circle, so 1 hour is 15 degrees). Declination runs from -90 degrees at the south pole of the sky to +90 at the north. The angles are tiny: a degree is 60 arcminutes and an arcminute is 60 arcseconds. The full Moon is about 1,800 arcseconds across. One pixel of a SPHEREx image covers 6.15 arcseconds.

2. Why some objects appear to move. Two effects shift a nearby object against the far background. Proper motion is the object's real movement through space seen from the side; it is only noticeable for objects close to us. Barnard's Star, six light years away, moves 10.4 arcseconds a year, the fastest of any star. Parallax is an apparent shift caused by the Earth going around the Sun, like a finger at arm's length jumping when you switch eyes. SPHEREx orbits the Earth, so pictures taken six months apart are taken from opposite sides of the Earth's orbit. Either way, movement means "close to us", and close objects are the ones we can study best.

3. Blinking. A blink comparator shows two photos of the same sky one after the other. Fixed stars stay still and movers jump. Clyde Tombaugh found Pluto this way in 1930, and volunteers in NASA's Backyard Worlds project have found hundreds of brown dwarfs using a computer version called WiseView, which the challenge points to as a model. Our tool is a blink comparator for SPHEREx.

4. The SPHEREx telescope. Launched in March 2025, SPHEREx maps the entire sky every six months in near-infrared light from 0.75 to 5.0 micrometres, which is invisible to human eyes (we see 0.4 to 0.7). It has six detectors, each covering one slice of that range. A special filter changes colour smoothly across each detector, so a star is measured at a slightly different wavelength each time it lands on a different spot. Over many exposures every point in the sky is seen in 102 colours. Each image file also carries a quality flag for every pixel, a model of the glow from interplanetary dust, and a table of the exact wavelength seen at every pixel.

5. Brown dwarfs and infrared colour. Brown dwarfs are too heavy to be planets and too light to shine like stars, so they slowly cool. The coldest known, WISE 0855-0714, is about -20 degrees Celsius. Cold objects give off most of their light at long infrared wavelengths, and the water and methane in their atmospheres absorb whole bands of colour. In our colour view (short wavelengths shown as blue, long as red) ordinary stars look blue-white and brown dwarfs look red.

6. Spectra. A spectrum is a graph of brightness against wavelength. Molecules absorb at specific wavelengths, so dips reveal what an atmosphere contains: water near 1.4, 1.9 and 2.7 micrometres, methane near 3.3, carbon dioxide near 4.3 and carbon monoxide near 4.6. Because each SPHEREx exposure measures the object at one colour, combining hundreds of exposures gives a full spectrum. Our chart shades the molecular bands and colours the points by sky pass, so a star that changes brightness splits into layers.

7. Saturation. A detector pixel fills up like a bucket. A star bright enough to fill it before the exposure ends is "saturated" and can no longer be measured. SPHEREx was built for faint galaxies, so bright stars saturate it. The SPHEREx data flags these pixels, and we never use them as measurements; the site says when a target is too bright to measure.

HOW IT WORKS

1. Find every exposure. We ask NASA's Infrared Science Archive (IRSA), through its standard Simple Image Access service, for every SPHEREx image that contains the position: usually 250 to 550 images across Data Release 1 and Quick Release 3.

2. Read only what is needed. Each image file is about 60 MB. Rather than download tens of gigabytes, we read only the few rows around the target straight from NASA's public copy of the archive on Amazon Web Services, using HTTP range requests. That is under 1 MB per image.

3. Clean each image. Using SPHEREx's own per-pixel flags we hide cosmic-ray hits, broken and hot pixels, afterglow from earlier bright stars, satellite streaks and other defects.

4. Group by sky pass. Images more than 60 days apart belong to different passes.

5. Align. Each image file describes how its pixels map onto the sky, including the optical distortion of the telescope. We resample every image onto one shared grid centred on the target, north up, with pixels half the native size so offset images fill in detail, and subtract the smooth glow of interplanetary dust.

6. Stack. For each pass and each detector we take the median of all aligned images, pixel by pixel. The median throws out stray bright pixels and lowers the noise, so one frame shows far fainter objects than a single exposure.

7. Draw. Sky images span a huge range of brightness, so we use an "asinh" stretch that shows faint and bright objects together, and we use one stretch for every pass of a field so that any change you see is real rather than a display effect.

8. Measure. For each exposure we find where the object should be on that date (from its known motion), add up its light in a small circle, subtract the surrounding sky, convert to millijanskys, and look up the wavelength SPHEREx measured at that exact pixel.

9. Overlay. Stars from ESA's Gaia catalogue are moved from their 2016 positions to each pass's date using Gaia's measured motions, then drawn as circles.

10. Publish. All of this is computed in advance for the five test objects, so the public site is just a fast static page and keeps working even when NASA's search service is busy. A small local server adds live lookups for any coordinates and spectra of any clicked point.

HOW WE CHECKED IT

We treated the five test objects as an exam with known answers. Barnard's Star moves about 11 arcseconds north between August 2025 and September 2026, exactly as published measurements predict, and Gaia's entry for it lands in the same place. The passes line up with each other to within 0.1 arcseconds, a fiftieth of a pixel. WISE 0855-0714 is detected at 4 to 5 micrometres at roughly the brightness its WISE catalogue entry predicts, looks red, and drifts along its predicted path. Epsilon Indi B moves over four passes, and its spectrum, built from about 340 exposures, shows the classic shape of a cool brown dwarf with a deep methane dip near 3.3 micrometres. RW Aurigae and R Draconis are too bright for SPHEREx in most or all exposures, and the site reports that honestly instead of drawing misleading numbers. Automated tests cover the motion calculation, the grouping into passes, the image orientation and the brightness stretch.

HOW IT ANSWERS THE CHALLENGE

The challenge asked for a public web tool where users enter coordinates and see a series of SPHEREx images like a little video, tested on Barnard's Star, Epsilon Indi B, WISE 0855, RW Aurigae and R Draconis. That is the core of VERIT-X, and all five targets are built in. Of the challenge's eight suggestions it covers seven: easy updates for new data releases (one line of code), creative use of the 102 bands (per-detector stacks, all-band stacks, colour composites and spectra on the fly), adding and subtracting images taken at different times, user-chosen field of view, a Gaia overlay, coordinates in the URL, and contamination metadata. It uses Astropy, as suggested. It does not yet overlay WISE images, and it uses its own viewer instead of Aladin so that it could control the flipbook, the shared brightness stretch and the spectra.

BENEFITS AND GOALS

Anyone with a browser can check any patch of sky for moving objects using NASA's newest all-sky data, with no installation and no account. Every new SPHEREx release adds a frame to every field, so the tool gets more sensitive over time. We hope it can support citizen science in the spirit of Backyard Worlds: volunteers flagging new brown dwarfs, nearby stars, asteroids and, perhaps one day, a Planet X.

LIMITS

Bright stars saturate, so their brightness can't be measured. There are only three or four passes per field so far. Spectrum fluxes are approximate (shape reliable, absolute level rough). Every star leaves a faint light-and-dark pair in the change view because SPHEREx's blur pattern differs slightly between passes. Live lookups of new coordinates need the local server and depend on NASA's search service.

TOOLS

Python 3.11 with Astropy 8.0.2, reproject 0.21.0, NumPy 2.4.6, SciPy 1.17.1, Pillow, requests, fsspec and aiohttp for the data pipeline; plain HTML, CSS and JavaScript for the website; FFmpeg for the demo video; GitHub Pages for hosting.
